<reason>Side B more convincingly argued that legally capping offsets would trigger "greenhushing"—firms abandoning net-zero claims while continuing emissions but ceasing to fund external abatement, thereby destroying billions in climate finance. Side B successfully distinguished between regulating offset quality versus quantity and exposed Side A's concession that dropping pledges "improves atmospheric integrity" as environmentally disastrous since operational emissions persist while offset funding evaporates. While Side A's moral hazard argument was compelling, it failed to adequately weigh the practical loss of verified climate finance that Side B demonstrated would result from the proposed cap.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 8) decisively contrasted the outcome of firms "exiting the claim" (continuing to emit while funding zero tons of removal) against the alternative of maintaining claims through verified offsets, exposing the proposition's perverse incentive to sacrifice real atmospheric benefit for marketing honesty.</best_rebuttal>
